project.name: The Eye and Sickle :: Rules engine
project.description:
THE RULES ENGINE. Not "the solo runtime" any more, despite the artifact id.
One implementation of the game's mechanics, driven two ways: the client drives it in process for single player, and a home server drives it for LAN and federated play. There is no second engine anywhere. Balance.java cites the design doc for every number, and a re-tune lands in every mode at once because there is only one place for it to land.
⚠ THE OLD DESCRIPTION HERE WAS A WARNING THAT IS NOW FALSE, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY. It said this module was "a second implementation of a subset of the game's rules", that single player used "a plain JSON save file", and that the module carried "no framework, no driver, no port, no daemon". The first stopped being true when the server was pointed at this engine instead of growing its own. The other two stopped being true on 2026-08-03, when the save system was unified: state now lives in `character_game_state`, in H2, written by ONE JdbcSaveStore in both modes, and this module carries an H2 driver, spring-jdbc and Flyway to do it.
WHAT THAT BOUGHT. The two stores were writing IDENTICAL BYTES — the state column is `text` holding the engine's own JSON document, opaque to SQL on purpose (see the V7 migration) — so the split bought two atomicity stories, two failure modes and two places for the save format to drift, and nothing else. Now: same migration, same store, same bytes, one code path.
WHAT IS STILL BANNED, AND WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW. No Spring Boot, no spring-web, no server module — see the enforcer rule below. A JDBC driver is a place to put bytes; a Boot context with a web layer is a second server, and the point of running the engine in-process is that single player does not need one. A second JVM running Boot costs roughly 200 MB of RSS and several seconds of startup, for a mode whose whole appeal is that you double-click and play.
THE INVARIANT THIS PRESERVES. I14 says game state never lives on player-controlled infrastructure. A solo save lives exactly there — so a solo character is LOCAL-ONLY AND CAN NEVER FEDERATE. ⚠ That protection was never the file format doing the work and is not weakened by the move to a database: a local H2 file is exactly as editable as JSON was, merely less pleasant to read. What holds the line is the quarantine rule (docs/architecture/12 §1), and nothing here may ever be trusted on the grounds that it came out of a database. docs/architecture/02 §4 recommends the same split ("local identity for solo play; a DID is required only to join a federated server"). Going online means a character created on a real home server, not an export of this one.

bannedDependencies.message:
The rules engine is a library, not a second server.
⚠ AMENDED 2026-08-03, AND THE AMENDMENT IS NARROW ON PURPOSE. This rule used to ban a database driver and a migration tool outright, on the grounds that "no second process, no database" was what justified the module. The save system is now shared with the server — one migration, one JdbcSaveStore, the same bytes — so H2, Flyway and spring-jdbc are permitted, and the justification is restated rather than dropped:
NO SECOND PROCESS. That is the property that mattered, and it is the one still enforced. A driver is a place to put bytes. Spring Boot with a web layer is a second server, and the whole point of running the engine in-process is that single player does not need one — a Boot JVM costs ~200 MB of RSS and several seconds of startup for a mode whose appeal is that you double-click and play.
So: spring-jdbc and its core are IN; all of Boot, spring-web and every HTTP stack stay OUT. The distinction is not "how much Spring" — it is whether this module could start listening on a port.
It must also never depend on eyeandsickle-server (rules are not authority) or eyeandsickle-client (rules do not import a view layer).
